 She’ll Get Another Social Security Raise in January. Medicaid Could Send Most of It to Her Nursing Home and Leave Her Just $50 a Month
 When Social Security sends a nursing-home resident a bigger check every January, Medicaid's rules quietly redirect nearly all of it before she sees a dime. The math behind what she actually keeps will surprise most families.
 By Gerelyn Terzo 
 Published October 30, 2026, 11:33am ET · 4 min read 
 The Full Benefits Desk desk. Editor: Gerelyn Terzo .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Medicaid's patient liability rule sends nearly all of a nursing-home resident's Social Security income to the facility, leaving her only her state's personal needs allowance.
 A widowed resident's $56 COLA raise in 2026 was entirely absorbed by a $17.90 Part B premium hike and a higher nursing-home payment, leaving her pocket money unchanged at $50.
 Families must monitor asset accumulation after each COLA, since uncollected patient-liability amounts can push residents past the $2,000 Medicaid asset cap and risk coverage loss.

 Global data center spending is expected to clinch $1 trillion in 2026 , and Anthropic’s IPO filing put fresh detail on the chip and server spending boom. Social Security checks are rising too. The newly announced 2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is 3.6%, after a 2.8% increase lifted the average retired worker’s benefit from $2,015 to $2,071 in 2026.
 For a nursing-home resident on Medicaid, most of that raise usually goes straight to the nursing home. Medicaid’s post-eligibility treatment of income rule, which families usually hear called the “patient liability” or “share of cost,” requires the resident to put nearly all of her monthly income toward her care after a short list of deductions. When the COLA raises her income, her payment goes up with it.
 How a Social Security Raise Turns Into a Bigger Nursing-Home Payment
 Once Medicaid covers a long-term nursing-home stay, the state doesn’t pay the whole bill. It first works out how much of the resident’s own income goes to the facility, and Medicaid pays the rest. Social Security, pensions, annuity payments and IRA distributions all count.
 That flips the usual logic of a raise. A bigger check can mean she pays more toward her care while Medicaid pays less, so much of the COLA may go toward the nursing-home bill.
 What She Keeps Before Medicaid Sets the Bill
 A few deductions come off the top before the state sets her payment:
 Personal needs allowance (PNA) . This is her spending money for haircuts, clothes and a phone bill. The federal minimum is $30, unchanged since the increase took effect in 1988. In 2026, the median state allowance is $70, with amounts ranging as high as $200.
 Health insurance premiums and uncovered medical costs. These expenses can shrink the income available for the nursing-home payment. When the resident pays her own Part B premium ($202.90 a month in 2026), for example, that premium lowers what she owes the nursing home.
 Spouse and family allowances. If her husband still lives at home, some of her income can go to him to bring his income up to a state floor. The federal minimum for that allowance rose to $2,705 a month in 2026.
 Whatever’s left goes to the nursing home. Those deductions depend heavily on where she lives. Alabama residents still keep just $30, while South Carolina raised its allowance to $60 in 2025. Some states regularly raise their PNA, while others haven’t changed it in decades.
 A $56 Raise That Leaves Her Pocket Money at $50
 Picture a widowed resident who gets the average retired worker benefit. She lives in a state with a flat $50 PNA and pays her own Part B premium. Here’s her math before and after the COLA:
 Monthly item 
 2025 
 2026 
 Social Security benefit 
 $2,015 
 $2,071 
 Personal needs allowance 
 $50 
 $50 
 Medicare Part B premium 
 $185 
 $202.90 
 Paid toward nursing-home care 
 $1,780 
 $1,818.10 
 Her check grew by $56. The Part B premium went up $17.90 and ate part of the raise. The other $38.10 went to the nursing home. Her spending money stayed at $50, which still won’t stretch to a decent winter coat. If her state tied its PNA to the COLA, she’d keep a little more.
 Why a Bigger Check Leaves the $2,000 Asset Limit Untouched
 Medicaid tests income and assets separately. The COLA raised her income but didn’t change the limit on what she can have in the bank. Many states cap a single resident’s countable assets at $2,000, the same limit SSI uses, and that figure didn’t change from 2025. California works differently: Medi-Cal brought back its asset test on January 1, 2026, with a $130,000 limit for one person through June 2027.
 The risk is income that piles up. Sometimes a family keeps paying last year’s patient-liability amount, or forgets to send the payment at all. The leftover money sits in her checking account, and if she is already near a $2,000 limit, even a few months of it can push her over and put coverage at risk.
 What Families Check After Every COLA
 The next round is already set. Social Security’s 2027 COLA will be 3.6%, with the higher payments beginning in January. Families that stay ahead of the paperwork check:
 The new gross Social Security amount on the SSA notice, which isn’t the same as the bank deposit
 The state’s current PNA and whether it rises with the COLA
 Medicare premium deductions, which change every January
 Spouse allowance figures, if a husband or wife still lives at home
 The state’s updated patient-liability notice, matched against the nursing home’s monthly bill
 The headline COLA percentage tells families very little. What matters is how many dollars of the raise the resident actually gets to keep, and in a state with a flat $50 allowance that number can be zero.
